sec1.lens: A table of contents is a promise to the reader — keep it clean, sequential, and let the architecture of the module itself do the selling.
emphasis: Signal that the Stack & Close is a craft, not a coercion
Frame the three sessions as a dignified progression: understand, build, refine
common_traps: Treating the TOC as filler rather than a trust-building roadmap
Rushing past the structural promise the TOC is making
voice_notes: Rather understated, really
The best closes feel like inevitable conclusions, not surprises

sec2.lens: Three readiness gates before you pitch — because a close delivered without rehearsal is a close delivered with apology in the voice.
emphasis: Rehearsal is the difference between sounding natural and sounding desperate
You cannot close with confidence on slides you haven't lived with
The word 'natural' in the checklist is doing enormous work — respect it
common_traps: Skipping rehearsal because the deck 'looks done'
Confusing familiarity with fluency
Treating the checklist as a formality rather than a gate
voice_notes: If it doesn't feel natural in rehearsal, it won't feel dignified on stage
The audience can always tell when you haven't earned your own offer yet

sec3.lens: This is the oversubscription mechanic dressed as a sequence — cumulative value, then a price that looks almost absurd by comparison, stated with calm.
emphasis: The human mind anchors on the last thing — so the last thing must be colossal value, not a minor bonus
The 4-step process is really one move: make perceived value outrun price by a factor that feels obvious
Transitions matter as much as content — the handover from teaching to offering is where trust is won or lost
common_traps: Spending the most energy on bonus #7 and throwing the core offer away in a sentence
Stacking features instead of cumulative value totals
A hard, awkward 'now I'm going to sell you something' transition that breaks the spell
voice_notes: Stack the value, then let the price fall — never the reverse
A billion dollars of sales isn't a coincidence, it's compounding arithmetic of perceived value
The close is a conclusion, not a pivot

sec4.lens: Story is the multiplier — same markers, same ink, ten-fold the price because a Tony Robbins anecdote reframed the object itself.
emphasis: Every stack item needs its own Hook to Story to Offer micro-structure, not just the headline offer
The story does the heavy lifting of perceived value; the offer is merely the container
Fit2Fat2Fit proves that a mediocre product with a magnificent hook will outsell a magnificent product with no hook
common_traps: Listing features and hoping price justifies itself
One big story for the whole stack instead of a story per component
Stories that are about you rather than about what the customer gets
voice_notes: Story is what turns a $10 marker into a $97 artifact
Never show an offer without a story — it's like serving wine without the glass
People don't buy products, they buy the meaning stories give them

sec5.lens: The workshop is a story-audit for every stack item — and the 'opportunity cost if they skip' question is the most important one on the sheet.
emphasis: Origin story, pain endured, and opportunity cost form the triangle of perceived value
If the creator can't articulate the pain behind a component, the audience will never feel its worth
Opportunity cost framing is the cleanest way to create urgency without pressure
common_traps: Fabricating pain when the real creation story is simpler and more honest
Skipping the opportunity-cost question because it feels uncomfortable
Writing feature descriptions instead of story arcs
voice_notes: What did it cost you to build this, truly?
If they walk away from this component, what life remains unlived?
The story must be earned, not manufactured

sec6.lens: A divider page that signals the shift from theory to craft — from understanding the stack to actually building it, slide by slide.
emphasis: The jump from framework to construction is where most practitioners stall
Session 2 is a builder's session — protect it from drift
common_traps: Treating the divider as decorative rather than as a mental gear-shift
Staying in theory mode when the workbook is asking for construction
voice_notes: Right, now we build

sec7.lens: Five slides to convert abstraction into cumulative, testable perceived value — and the 'Get Rid Of' slide is the quiet weapon everyone underestimates.
emphasis: The 'what they won't have to do anymore' slide carries as much persuasive weight as the feature list
Every stack iteration must end with a Total Value number — the escalation is the mechanic
This five-slide pattern is a template, not a one-off — the audience learns the rhythm and anticipates the payoff
common_traps: Skipping the capabilities slide and going straight to price
Vague 'Get Rid Of' lists that don't name specific tools, costs, or frictions
Inconsistent Total Value escalation that breaks the pattern the audience has learned
voice_notes: Tell them what they gain, then tell them what they get to put down
Each stack recap should land heavier than the last
The template is the trust — deviate from it and you break the spell

sec8.lens: Four products, four braindumps, each with testimonials and concern-resolution baked in — this is where oversubscription is earned, not claimed.
emphasis: Testimonials and concern-resolution are load-bearing inside each stack, not reserved for the close
Each product needs its own origin story — no shortcuts, no shared narrative
The slide-range mapping (64-72, 73-78, etc.) is the discipline that keeps construction on-rail
common_traps: Reusing the same testimonial across multiple stack items
Treating products 2-5 as filler rather than cumulative proof of generosity
Writing once and moving on rather than iterating each braindump with the same rigour
voice_notes: Four stories, four stacks, four moments where you could have lost them — don't
Each component must earn its place with its own testimony
Generosity is a structural decision, not a feeling

sec9.lens: The 'If All' statements are the polite knock before you walk in with the price — three yeses in a row make the number inevitable rather than startling.
emphasis: Trial closes from the start so the price moment isn't a sudden ask
Three If-All statements — Vehicle, Internal, External — cover functional, emotional, and practical framings of worth
Scarcity must have a reason — 'only today' without a why feels manipulative; with a why it feels considered
common_traps: Delivering If-All statements rhetorically without actually waiting for the audience to verbally agree
Using manufactured scarcity that insults the audience's intelligence
Launching the price cold, without the three-yes staircase in front of it
voice_notes: Would it be worth it? Genuinely wait for the nod
A price stated after three agreements feels inevitable; a price stated cold feels aggressive
Scarcity done clean is simply honouring the structure of the offer

sec10.lens: Four objection tools — Price Justification, Two Choices, Guarantee, Real Question — each a dignifying invitation rather than a pressure tactic, if delivered with calm.
emphasis: The guarantee reversal ('30 hours, 31 hours, 32 hours and 59 minutes') is warmth — it signals you trust them
The Real Question reframes risk: not 'will this work?' but 'what's the risk of not finding out?'
'Two Choices' framing must avoid shaming option 1 — contrast, not contempt
common_traps: Price justifications that compare the offer to luxuries they don't care about
Guarantees that read as legal boilerplate rather than personal assurance
Making 'Choice 1' sound pathetic — it breaks dignity and reduces conversion
The Real Question delivered as a rhetorical trick rather than a genuine reframe
voice_notes: The guarantee should sound like a friend, not a contract
If they saw how you handled their objection, would they feel respected?
The real question is always: what does this cost you if you don't find out?
Contrast the two choices with neutrality — never with scorn

sec11.lens: The recap stack, a fast-mover bonus for momentum, and a CTA that names the exact action — three slides that close a two-hour conversation in ninety seconds if built right.
emphasis: Recap stack is the final total-value moment — it must land with the weight of everything preceding it
Fast Movers Bonus should reward decisiveness, not punish deliberation
The CTA must be surgically specific — 'Submit Application with 50% deposit' beats 'sign up today'
common_traps: A recap stack that looks rushed or differently-styled from the earlier stack slides
Fast-movers bonuses that feel like bribes rather than rewards for trust
Vague CTAs ('Get Started') that leave the hand hovering over the button
voice_notes: Tell them exactly what happens next — no ambiguity is a kindness
The bonus for acting fast honours the ones who trust you quickly
The last slide is the handshake — make it clean

sec12.lens: Ninety percent of sales come after the price — a number that should humble anyone who thinks the close ends when the number is revealed.
emphasis: The presentation doesn't end at the price reveal — it pivots into sustained engagement
Most practitioners lose the room in the twenty minutes after the price because they stop selling and start waiting
The reflection prompt is an opportunity for honest self-audit — have you built enough to hold the room post-reveal?
common_traps: Mentally 'landing the plane' at the price and allowing energy to drop
Not preparing Session 3 material and scrambling live
Treating the post-price time as buffer rather than as the highest-leverage sales window of the entire event
voice_notes: Nine out of ten yeses come after the price — so the real work begins once the number is spoken
The close is not a finish line, it's a midpoint

sec13.lens: Four post-reveal amplifiers — Q&A with countdown, pre-built questions, live success stories, and 'You're probably thinking this' — each designed to hold the room with grace rather than grip.
emphasis: Pre-built FAQ slides are not manipulation, they are respect — you've anticipated the hesitation
Countdown clock creates structure, not pressure, if paired with substantive content
'You're probably thinking this' is the single most disarming phrase in a close when used with warmth
Live student stories post-price outperform every other persuasion tactic in the room
common_traps: Q&A that invites a loud skeptic to dominate the room
Countdown clock with no substance behind it — feels like a cheap sales tactic
'You're probably thinking this' delivered with condescension rather than empathy
Scripting student stories so tightly they feel performed
voice_notes: Prepare the top thirty questions — if you don't know them, you haven't sold this offer enough times yet
The countdown is a container, not a whip
Let your students speak — their words carry a trust yours cannot
You're probably thinking this — and you'd be right to

sec14.lens: Record yourself, watch yourself, cringe appropriately, then refine — the discipline most presenters skip because it's uncomfortable, which is precisely why it works.
emphasis: Recording and reviewing is the single highest-leverage rehearsal step
Polishing stories and images is not cosmetic — it's where congruence is built
Smooth delivery comes from discomfort tolerated in private
common_traps: Rehearsing mentally rather than out loud on camera
Reviewing the recording once and moving on
Treating the homework as optional because 'the deck is done'
voice_notes: Watch yourself back — that's where the work is
The polish is the respect you pay the audience
Rehearsal isn't about the words, it's about the room you'll be in

sec15.lens: Back matter — the quiet close of the workbook itself, a reminder that good craft ends with a considered pause rather than a flourish.
emphasis: Even back-cover design signals care to the reader
common_traps: Overlooking the final page as irrelevant
voice_notes: Let the final page breathe
